structured_output.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the measured free surface of a resting biconcave mammalian red blood cell has a mean curvature H that varies substantially from point to point (it is not constant), and cells in hypotonic or diluted medium relax to a sphere (constant H).
structured_output.pass_criterion: In at least 90% of reconstructed 3D surfaces of discocyte red cells in isotonic plasma or buffer, the coefficient of variation of mean curvature H over the membrane surface (excluding a 5% boundary margin) is at least 0.5. The same cells must also become spherical, with sphericity index at least 0.95, after dilution in hypotonic medium.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if, in more than 25% of isotonic discocytes, the coefficient of variation of H over the surface is below 0.15, which is within reconstruction noise of constant mean curvature. It is also refuted if the cells do not become spherical on dilution.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'surface of equilibrium' for surface tension alone is a surface of constant mean curvature (the Delaunay unduloid, nodoid, and so on). The test therefore measures the spatial variation of H on 3D red-cell surfaces from tomographic or holographic reconstructions. Thompson's 'diluted blood' maps to hypotonic medium. His 'osmotic inequilibrium' and 'fluid-crystal forces' correspond to modern bilayer-couple, spectrin-cytoskeleton elasticity and bending-energy models (Helfrich). The modern reinterpretation is that H is not constant because the membrane has bending rigidity and shear elasticity, not because of cholesterin liquid crystals. This does not alter the geometric test. A caveat is that the Laplace pressure balance of an osmotically pressurised drop also gives constant H. The test is therefore of the shape, not of the mechanism.
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: I could not verify, with a title, URL and DOI I am sure resolve, any public dataset of 3D red-blood-cell surface reconstructions. Such a dataset would need isotonic and hypotonic cells with a per-cell surface mesh or height map. Most published quantitative phase imaging and tomography data on red cells are either not deposited or are in paper supplements I cannot confirm. Under the rule against fabricating identifiers, I am returning null rather than guessing. The geometric part of the claim, that the biconcave profile is not a constant-mean-curvature surface, can also be settled analytically from the standard Evans-Fung biconcave profile. That is a calculation, not a dataset.
